name: NMN
summary: Nicotinamide mononucleotide, a building block the body uses to make NAD+, taken in hopes of slowing aging and boosting metabolism; human benefits are unproven.
what_it_is: NMN (nicotinamide mononucleotide) is a form of vitamin B3 that cells can turn into NAD+, a coenzyme used in the chemical reactions that release energy from food. NAD+ levels fall with age in mammals, and in mice NMN improved glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity, which led to its promotion as an anti-aging supplement. Some NMN taken by mouth is converted to nicotinamide before it reaches the bloodstream, and how it enters cells is still debated.

evidence.why: Eight small randomized trials in 342 mostly healthy adults, lasting up to 12 weeks, found NMN raised blood NAD+ in most but did not improve blood sugar, cholesterol, BMI or blood pressure.

status_us.label: Dietary supplement since FDA's September 2025 reversal
status_us.note: FDA said in late 2022 that NMN could not be a dietary supplement because it had first been investigated as a drug, then reversed that position in letters dated September 29 and December 2, 2025. NMN is still a new dietary ingredient, so a premarket notification to FDA is required.

benefits.claim: Raised blood NAD+ in 5 of 8 small randomized trials in adults; whether it also raises NAD+ inside cells and tissues is unclear
No improvement in fasting blood sugar, insulin, HbA1c, blood fats, BMI or blood pressure versus placebo across 8 trials of 14 days to 12 weeks in 342 adults
Better muscle insulin sensitivity in the only trial of people with prediabetes, which enrolled women

risks.risk: Long-term safety is uncertain, especially at higher amounts and in older adults; the longest trials lasted 12 weeks
No serious side effects were reported in trials, but adverse events tended to be more frequent in the higher-dose groups of two trials
Theoretical concerns raised by reviewers: higher NAD+ might feed tumor growth or harmful signals from aging cells, and its by-product nicotinamide has a possible link with heart disease risk

avoid_if: Current or past cancer (clinician first, given a theoretical concern about tumor growth)

labs.why: No routine tests are needed and no evidence-based monitoring exists; trials found no changes in liver enzymes, BMI or blood pressure.

studies.title: Effects of Nicotinamide Mononucleotide on Glucose and Lipid Metabolism in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomised Controlled Trials
studies.people: 342 adults in 8 randomized trials in Japan, India and the US, mostly healthy and middle-aged or older
studies.finding: NMN did not improve fasting glucose, insulin, HbA1c, blood fats, BMI or blood pressure; a borderline drop in insulin resistance disappeared when one trial was removed. The authors say the results do not support NMN for the general population.

studies.title: Dietary Supplementation With NAD+-Boosting Compounds in Humans: Current Knowledge and Future Directions
studies.people: Human trials of NR, NMN and related compounds in healthy midlife and older adults and some patient groups
studies.finding: These supplements appear safe and can raise NAD+ in several tissues, but evidence that they improve how the body functions is unclear, and small trials limit conclusions.

ask_your_clinician: Is there any reason, such as a past cancer, that I should avoid NAD+ boosters?
Since trials found no change in blood sugar or cholesterol, how would we tell whether NMN is doing anything for me?
Which proven steps should come first for my metabolic or healthy-aging goals?

notes_for_editor: Trials were small (14 to 108 people), short (14 days to 12 weeks) and mostly in Asia; their funding sources were in a supplementary table that was not opened. The cancer and heart concerns are theoretical points from the meta-analysis discussion, not trial findings. FDA's 2025 letters themselves were not opened; the status rests on a law-firm summary and a trade-news report, which agree with each other and with nad.json. The meta-analysis was accepted in October 2024 and appears in the journal's 2025 volume. The NAD+ booster review was read only as an abstract.
